/meta/title: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
/meta/subtitle: Five lives, two sides of a bridge
/meta/adaptedFrom: Adapted from Thornton Wilder’s Pulitzer Prize–winning novel
/meta/tagline: When fate offers no explanation, how can we go on loving?
/frame/levelIntro/1/1/text: At noon that day, I was approaching the bridge. The road beneath my feet was white with heat, and five people had already stepped onto the planks. Then the bridge, like a string held taut too long, snapped into the gorge. I stood so close to them, and yet I was still alive. Had they merely arrived a few moments before me?
/frame/levelIntro/1/2/text: I believe there is an order to the world. But believing is one thing; facing five deaths is another. I wanted to know how they had lived, whom they had known, whom they had loved. If I could discover all this, might I also understand why it had been these five?
/frame/levelIntro/1/3/text: First, someone told me that the old woman who died was very strange. Some remembered her drinking, others her learning. Others still remembered how a letter from Spain could make her seem a different person. I heard many accounts of the same woman that scarcely resembled one another.
/frame/levelIntro/1/4/text: Her daughter lived across the sea; beside her lived a girl without parents. Both had letters they wished to write, things they could not say. I would begin with that house, and listen for voices that had never reached the street. Can someone’s hunger for love exhaust the very people who love them?
/frame/levelIntro/2/1/text: People in the city were always mistaking us for one another. They would laugh, try the other name, and we would go on with our work. Explaining was tiring; sometimes it was easier to let them talk. As long as my brother stood beside me, I knew their mistakes had not really made either of us disappear.
/frame/levelIntro/2/2/text: We scrubbed church walls, copied plays for the theatre, and carried cargo at the shore. At the end of a day, neither had to tell the whole story for the other to know why he was tired. Sometimes we walked the same road separately, so that people would not stop to make jokes again.
/frame/levelIntro/2/3/text: Later, he kept going past the theatre and came home later than before. I waited at the table while the candle grew shorter. The life I had thought complete could evidently make room for someone else. I did not understand the change, or know how to ask him about it without sounding accusing.
/frame/levelIntro/2/4/text: Later still, someone asked which one I was. I understood perfectly, but gave the other name. Once the answer left my mouth, people were still waiting for me to move on. Standing alone where two people used to live, how can a person know where to go next?
/frame/levelIntro/3/1/text: The first time I slept in that little bed, I was not thinking of fame. There was hot soup. I was no longer locked up. Someone was teaching me to sing. That alone meant my life had changed. Later, everyone remembered me on the stage; hardly anyone asked about the little girl who had come out of the café.
/frame/levelIntro/3/2/text: He taught me to understand a line, to turn, to let my voice pause in just the right place. The warmer the audience became, the more I dreaded returning to my dressing room and finding him whistling in a corner. It was as though everyone else’s approval together could not buy one reassuring word from him.
/frame/levelIntro/3/3/text: I thought of leaving the stage, becoming a respectable woman, being a mother to my children. But each new life I entered was followed by someone calling me by an old name. Even if he had helped me, even if I had once been deeply grateful, that did not mean every door could forever be opened without knocking.
/frame/levelIntro/3/4/text: Now he has come again, asking to take my child into the city for a year. He says he can teach him many things. I know he can. I also know how frail my boy is. When someone wishes to offer care, should they not pause to hear the answer of the person they would care for?
/frame/ending/segments/0/text: All five who stepped onto the bridge came from somewhere, and all had things left undone. A letter remained across the sea. A voyage had not begun. Rooms in the city were waiting to be put in order. When the bridge broke, these unfinished things did not become an explanation for the disaster.
/frame/ending/segments/1/text: Brother Juniper investigated for six years. He recorded every detail he heard, afraid that one omitted fact might mean a lost answer. The cook remembered what María ate; the bookseller spoke of her learning; others remembered an eccentric, tiresome woman. Even those closest to the dead had things they could not put into words.
/frame/ending/segments/2/text: Earlier, during a plague, he had made a table of fifteen people who died and fifteen who survived, comparing their goodness, piety, and usefulness to their families. The results did not support the explanation he expected. He tore up the paper and cast it into the sea, then recovered his faith from the beauty of sea and sky. That table had never concerned the five people on the bridge.
/frame/ending/segments/3/text: At last his book about the bridge was finished. It was condemned as heresy, to be burned together with its author. On his last night, the friar still wondered where the plan for his own life lay. At least one wish was clear: he hoped someone would believe that he had begun his inquiry for the sake of faith. In the square, some people did believe him.
/frame/ending/segments/4/text: Now look back six years, to the memorial service after the collapse. Black veils, candles, silver, and singing filled the church. The captain stayed only a little while, then went down to the sea. Sitting among the girls, the abbess thought of Pepita. She admitted that she had been too busy, and had placed too many hopes for her work upon that child.
/frame/ending/segments/5/text: Camila had meant to attend as well. On the way, thinking of the crowd, the ceremony, and the faces already growing indistinct, she stopped in a little church. She thought she could feel nothing. Then anguish came: she could never tell Pio that she loved him, never give Jaime fresh courage when he was suffering. She returned to her villa.
/frame/ending/segments/6/text: A year later, she heard that the abbess had lost two people close to her in the same accident. At first she hid near the convent, watching that plain face. At last she went inside and confessed that she was the former actress. Before she could finish speaking, she bent beneath her grief.
/frame/ending/segments/7/text: Mother, what shall I do? I am all alone. I have nothing. I loved them. What shall I do?
/frame/ending/segments/8/text: The abbess did not immediately offer an explanation. She led Camila into the garden, sent for water, spoke of the nun who tended the flowers, and then asked about the child and friend she had lost. The grief Camila had carried for years had finally found somewhere to rest, without a defense or a performance.
/frame/ending/segments/9/text: Later, Clara came from Spain, bringing her mother’s last letter to the convent. She struggled to defend her mother, and blamed herself. Reading the letter, the abbess was astonished that such generous sentences had come from someone she had once dismissed. She asked the daughter to stay and see their daily work.
/frame/ending/segments/10/text: The sun went down, and lamps lit corridor after corridor. Old people, children, the sick, and the blind were here. The abbess still wanted to know whether someone could devise a language for the deaf, whether there were gentler ways of caring for people whose minds were troubled. She was old, yet still asking what could be done next.
/frame/ending/segments/11/text: Camila was now among her helpers, about to go on an errand across the city. The abbess must still say a few words in the sickroom, then bargain with the flour merchant who was growing impatient. The lamp was set on the floor. The patients looked at her. Outside it was dark; inside, someone stayed to offer a little light and warmth.
/frame/ending/segments/12/text: The abbess thought that, in time, even those who remembered the five would die. Those who had loved them would be loved a little longer, and would also be forgotten. Yet the love had existed. The heart’s reaching toward another did not depend upon being remembered forever.
/frame/ending/segments/13/text: There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning.
/frame/ending/credit: Adapted from Thornton Wilder’s The Bridge of San Luis Rey, published in 1927 and awarded the 1928 Pulitzer Prize for the Novel. Interior voices and scenes are abridged or reconstructed. The final sentence follows the original English.
